'''Harry Kesten''' (November 19, 1931 – March 29, 2019) was a Jewish American mathematician best known for his work in [[probability]], most notably on [[random walk]]s on [[Group (mathematics)|group]]s and [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]], [[random matrix|random matrices]], [[branching process]]es, and [[percolation theory]].

== Biography ==

Harry Kesten was born in Duisburg, Germany in 1931,<ref name = ":1">{{cite journal | last1 = Grimmett| first1 = Geoffrey R. | last2 = Lawler| first2 = Gregory F. |date=June 2020 | title = Harry Kesten (1931–2019): A Personal and Scientific Tribute | journal = [[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] | volume = 67 | issue = 6 | pages = 822–831 | url = https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/202006/rnoti-p822.pdf |doi = 10.1090/noti2100| doi-access = free}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> and grew up in the [[History of the Jews in the Netherlands|Netherlands]], where he moved with his parents in 1933 to escape the [[Nazi]]s. Surviving [[The Holocaust in the Netherlands|the Holocaust]], Kesten initially studied chemistry, and later theoretical physics and mathematics, at the [[University of Amsterdam]]. He moved to the [[United States]] in 1956 and received his PhD in mathematics in 1958 at [[Cornell University]] under the supervision of [[Mark Kac]].  He was an instructor at [[Princeton University]] and the [[Hebrew University]] before returning to Cornell in 1961.<ref name=":1"></ref>

Kesten died on March 29, 2019, in [[Ithaca, New York|Ithaca]] at the age of 87.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Probability expert Harry Kesten, PhD '58, dies at 87 |url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2019/04/probability-expert-harry-kesten-phd-58-dies-87 |website=Cornell Chronicle |access-date=April 19, 2019 |language=en}}</ref>

== Mathematical work ==
Kesten's work includes many fundamental contributions across almost the whole of probability,<ref name=":1"></ref><ref>{{cite journal | author = Grimmett, G. R. | year = 2021 | title = Harry Kesten's work in probability theory | journal = Probab. Th. Rel. Fields | volume = 181 | issue = 1–3 | pages = 17–56 | doi = 10.1007/s00440-021-01046-4 | arxiv = 2004.03861 }}</ref><ref>Durrett, R., Harry Kesten's publications: a personal perspective. Perplexing problems in probability, 1–33, Progr. Probab., 44, Birkhäuser, Boston MA, 1999.</ref> including the following highlights.

*''[[Random walks]] on [[Group (mathematics)|groups]].''  In his 1958 PhD thesis, Kesten studied symmetric random walks on countable groups ''G''  generated by a jump distribution with support ''G''. He showed that the spectral radius equals the exponential decay rate of the return probabilities.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Kesten, H. | year = 1959 | title = Symmetric random walks on groups | journal = Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. | volume = 92 | issue = 2| pages = 336–354 | doi=10.1090/s0002-9947-1959-0109367-6| doi-access = free }}</ref>  He showed later that this is strictly less than 1 if and only if the group is [[amenable group|non-amenable]].<ref>Kesten, H., Full Banach mean values on countable groups. Math. Scand. 7 (1959), 146–156.</ref> The last result is known as ''Kesten's criterion for amenability''. He calculated the spectral radius of the ''d''-regular tree, namely  <math>\frac{2\sqrt{d-1}}{d}</math>.
*''Products of [[random matrices]].'' Let <math>Y_n=X_1 X_2\cdots X_n</math> be the product of the first ''n'' elements of an ergodic stationary sequence of random <math>k \times k</math> matrices.  With [[Hillel Furstenberg|Furstenberg]] in 1960, Kesten showed the convergence of <math>n^{-1}\log^+\|Y_n\|</math>, under the condition <math>E (\log^+\|X_1\|)<\infty</math>.<ref>Furstenberg, H. and Kesten, H., Products of random matrices, Ann. Math. Statist. 31 (1960), 457–469.</ref>
*''[[Self-avoiding walks]].''  Kesten's ratio limit theorem states that the number <math>\sigma_n</math> of ''n''-step self-avoiding walks from the origin on the integer lattice satisfies <math> \sigma_{n+2}/\sigma_n \to \mu^2</math> where <math>\mu</math> is the [[connective constant]].  This result remains unimproved despite much effort.<ref>Madras, N. and Slade, G., The self-avoiding walk, Birkhäuser, Boston, 1993.</ref> In his proof, Kesten proved his pattern theorem, which states that, for a proper internal pattern ''P'', there exists <math>\alpha</math> such that the proportion of walks containing fewer than <math>\alpha n</math> copies of ''P'' is exponentially smaller than <math>\sigma_n</math>.<ref>Kesten, H., On the number of self-avoiding walks. I and II. J. Math. Phys. 4 (1963) 960–969,  5  (1964), 1128–1137.</ref>
*''[[Branching process]]es.'' Kesten and Stigum showed that the correct condition for the convergence of the population size, normalized by its mean, is that <math>E(L\log^+ L)<\infty</math> where ''L'' is a typical family size.<ref>Kesten, H. and Stigum, B,  A limit theorem for multidimensional Galton–Watson processes,
Ann. Math. Statist. 37 (1966), 1211–1223.</ref>  With Ney and [[Frank Spitzer|Spitzer]], Kesten found the minimal conditions for the asymptotic distributional properties of a critical branching process, as discovered earlier, but subject to stronger assumptions, by [[Kolmogorov]] and [[Akiva Yaglom|Yaglom]].<ref>Kesten, H., Ney, P. and Spitzer, F., The Galton–Watson process with mean one and finite variance, Theory Probab. Appl. 11 (1966), 513–540.</ref>

*''[[Random walk]] in a random environment.'' With Kozlov and [[Frank Spitzer|Spitzer]], Kesten proved a deep theorem about random walk in a one-dimensional random environment.  They established the limit laws for the walk across the variety of situations that can arise within the environment.<ref>Kesten, H., Kozlov, M. V., Spitzer, F. A limit law for random walk in a random environment. Compositio Math. 30 (1975), 145–168.</ref>
* ''[[Diophantine approximation]].'' In 1966, Kesten resolved a conjecture of [[Paul Erdős|Erdős]] and Szűsz on the discrepancy of irrational rotations. He studied the discrepancy between the number of rotations by <math>\xi</math> hitting a given interval ''I'', and the length of ''I'', and proved this bounded if and only if the length of ''I'' is a multiple of <math>\xi</math>.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Kesten, H.|title=On a conjecture of Erdős and Szüsz related to uniform distribution mod 1|journal=Acta Arith.|volume=12|date=1966|issue=2 |pages=193–212|url=https://eudml.org/doc/204796|doi=10.4064/aa-12-2-193-212|doi-access=free}}</ref>
*''[[Diffusion-limited aggregation]].'' Kesten proved that the growth rate of the arms in ''d'' dimensions can be no larger than <math>n^{2/(d+1)}</math>.<ref>Kesten, H., How long are the arms in DLA?  J. Phys. A  20  (1987),   L29–L33.</ref><ref>Kesten, H., Upper bounds for the growth rate of DLA, Physica A 168 (1990), 529–535.</ref>
*''[[percolation theory|Percolation]].'' Kesten's most famous work in this area is his proof that the critical probability of bond percolation on the square lattice equals 1/2.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Kesten, H. | year = 1980 | title = The critical probability of bond percolation on the square lattice equals 1/2 | journal = Comm. Math. Phys. | volume = 74 | issue = 1| pages = 41–59 | doi=10.1007/bf01197577| bibcode = 1980CMaPh..74...41K| s2cid = 3143683 }}</ref> He followed this with a systematic study of percolation in two dimensions, reported in his book ''Percolation Theory for Mathematicians''.<ref>{{Citation | author= Kesten, H. | title= Percolation Theory for Mathematicians | year =1982 | url = https://www.math.cornell.edu/~kesten/kesten-book.html}}.</ref> His work on scaling theory and scaling relations<ref>{{cite journal | author = Kesten, H. | year = 1987 | title = Scaling relations for 2D-percolation | url = http://purl.umn.edu/4435| journal = Comm. Math. Phys. | volume = 109 | issue = 1| pages = 109–156 | doi=10.1007/bf01205674| bibcode = 1987CMaPh.109..109K| s2cid = 118713698 }}</ref> has since proved key to the relationship between critical percolation and [[Schramm–Loewner evolution]].<ref>{{cite journal | author = Smirnov S | year = 2001 | title = Critical percolation in the plane: conformal invariance, Cardy's formula, scaling limits | journal = Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, Série I | volume = 333 | issue = 3| pages = 239–244 | doi=10.1016/s0764-4442(01)01991-7 | bibcode=2001CRASM.333..239S| arxiv = 0909.4499}}</ref>
*''[[First passage percolation]].'' Kesten's results for this growth model are largely summarized in ''Aspects of First Passage Percolation''.<ref>Kesten, H., Aspects of First Passage Percolation. École d'été de probabilités de Saint-Flour, XIV—1984, 125–264, Lecture Notes in Math., 1180, Springer, Berlin, 1986.</ref> He studied the rate of convergence to the time constant, and contributed to the topics of [[subadditivity|subadditive]] stochastic processes and [[concentration of measure]]. He developed the problem of [[maximum flow]] through a medium subject to random capacities.

A volume of papers was published in Kesten's honor in 1999.<ref>Perplexing problems in probability: Festschrift in honor of Harry Kesten, Bramson, M. and Durrett, R., eds, Progr. Probab., 44, Birkhäuser, Boston MA, 1999</ref> The Kesten memorial volume of [[Probability Theory and Related Fields]]<ref>{{cite journal | editor = H. Duminil-Copin, G. R. Grimmett | title=Special issue in honor of the life and work of Harry Kesten | journal=Probability Theory and Related Fields | volume=181 | year=2021 | pages = 1–756}}</ref> contains a full list of the dedicatee's publications.
